unresolved_added: The national mortality framing establishes importance but does not validate the county model.
The source alternates between opioid use, abuse, drug reports, infected individuals, and health; these are not interchangeable outcomes.
Police laboratory reports measure investigations and reporting practice, not true prevalence.
Legitimate prescriptions, illicit use, addiction, and overdose are combined without a full observation model.
The official problem statement is not reproduced, so task reconstruction remains paper-internal.
The Summary calls the model robust and accurate before the body presents validation.
The claimed ability to scale to larger regions is not tested.
The disease metaphor can obscure social, medical, market, and enforcement mechanisms.
Setting a missing county-year drug report to zero can turn missingness into false absence.
Bedford City/County merging needs a population, FIPS, and temporal reconciliation audit.
Manual reconciliation of Census category splits is not accompanied by a mapping table.
The 134, 149, 150, and 152 socioeconomic-factor counts require a versioned feature lineage.
The county-distance data are measured for 2010 and treated as fixed without documenting the distance definition.
Treating each drug report as an infected individual ignores multiple reports, seizures, specimens, and enforcement intensity.
The positive-feedback addiction story does not establish county-level contagion.
Second-order Markov memory is chosen for computational convenience without lag comparison.
Prior Markov applications in population and epidemiology do not validate this deterministic opioid transition.
The inverse relation with distance is hypothesized a priori and not compared with alternatives.
The distance adjacency uses reciprocal distance without a stated unit, scaling rule, or zero-distance guard.
Self-influence is fixed to one, which may be incomparable with reciprocal intercounty distances.
All opioids are treated as identical despite different potency, supply, prescription, and temporal patterns.
Sparse drug-specific reports motivate pooling but the resulting aggregation bias is not quantified.
Assuming all opioid addictions are cured in the same manner is medically and operationally implausible.
Homogeneous reporting accuracy across counties is explicitly unverifiable and likely false.
Per-capita normalization does not correct underreporting or differential enforcement.
The health notation calls drug reports `health`, reversing the usual direction and risking interpretation errors.
The state `x_t = 2n_t-n_(t-1)` can be negative and no nonnegativity handling is reported.
Equation 1 is a conceptual decomposition without scale reconciliation between surrounding problem and internal well-being.
`Q` has N-squared parameters with only a few annual transitions, creating severe identifiability risk.
The optimization in Equation 3 does not state whether norms are squared, weighted, regularized, or constrained.
Row normalization of Q is mentioned after fitting but its timing and effect are not specified.
Column sums of normalized Q may conflate network size, scaling, self-effects, and direction.
The model does not distinguish incoming from outgoing influence, as the authors later admit.
The finite five-state boundary gives edge counties unmodeled neighbors and distorted influence.
Top-30 Pearson screening is performed with outcome data and no held-out selection procedure.
Correlation magnitudes are not accompanied by signs, confidence intervals, multiplicity control, or stability.
Many selected factors are raw population counts, so total population can drive spurious correlation.
The feature list includes ancestry and language variables with serious confounding and policy-ethics risks.
The linear model has no intercept, scaling, regularization, residual diagnostics, or coefficient table in the paper.
The logistic model has no coefficient, calibration, uncertainty, or regularization report.
The infection threshold assumes approximate normality without a distribution check.
Mean plus one standard deviation is said to select the top 16 percent, but the empirical share is about 12 percent.
The threshold is fixed from 2010 despite changing reporting and population conditions.
Values just below the threshold receive no priority, producing a cliff effect.
The initial 2010-2015 fit and 2016 error may still be in-sample through shared Q estimation choices.
The exact scientific-notation exponents are visually recoverable but vulnerable to text extraction loss and must be bound to rasters.
The two-year training test is stronger than the first fit but remains one temporal split with no uncertainty.
Long-run propagation to all counties cured by 2025 is inconsistent with later policy urgency and needs reconciliation.
Convergence to the initial mean may be a mathematical consequence of normalization rather than empirical epidemic behavior.
The R-squared value 0.1296 supports weak aggregate fit but does not prove human behavior is inherently unpredictable.
The internal-model forecast error is compared with the external model without a full unit and information-parity audit.
Logistic accuracy 87.98 percent is misleading under 12 percent positives; the authors correctly reveal this but do not report precision or false-positive counts.
True-positive rate 3.57 percent indicates near-total failure at the default cutoff.
Lowering the probability threshold to 0.1 captures 70 percent of infected counties but omits specificity, precision, workload, and calibration.
The prose changes the two-stage one-model-positive label from medium risk to low risk.
The convex search uses a 0.001 grid but does not standardize branch outputs or cross-validate theta.
Theta equal to one means the proposed convex combination contributes no socioeconomic prediction.
Claiming socioeconomic information is already encoded in current reports is plausible but not identified.
The two-stage model cannot forecast beyond 2016 because socioeconomic inputs end.
The decline to zero high-risk counties may reflect threshold mechanics or branch collapse rather than stabilization.
Epicenters are defined and then judged against maps derived from related data, so the visual check is not independent validation.
Selecting exactly ten epicenters and ten vulnerable counties is not calibrated to capacity or error.
Hadamard Q-times-A, matrix QA, Q alone, and absolute Q produce different appendix rankings.
Mecklenburg is explained through omitted neighboring states, but no outside-state data test the explanation.
Highway alignment is visually suggestive but road traffic, direction, interdiction, and drug-flow data are absent.
Setting epicenter health to zero is an extreme and infeasible intervention.
Setting distances to and from epicenters to zero is mathematically described as border control but conflicts with reciprocal-distance semantics.
Zeroing Q entries may change both incoming and outgoing effects depending on index orientation.
The 7-versus-56 and 8-versus-56 simulation counts have no uncertainty or robustness region.
Halving demographic fractions can create impossible joint populations and breaks compositional constraints.
Large sensitivity responses from the weak internal classifier should not be read as causal intervention effects.
Explanations involving seniors, teenagers, marriage, veterans, education, and labor are speculative and may stigmatize groups.
Calling intuitive trends evidence of generalization confuses plausibility with out-of-sample performance.
Strength claims such as `incredibly accurate` and `generalize to all areas and problems` overstate the evidence.

The weakness section correctly identifies directional flow, edge effects, threshold cliffs, missing prioritization cost, socioeconomic contradiction, and feedback omission; none is repaired in the reported model.
Policy proposals inherit correlations and extreme simulations without causal estimates, costs, uptake, equity, legal authority, or monitoring.
Border checkpoints may impose major civil, legal, economic, and distributional burdens not analyzed.
The DEA letter converts demographic edits into advertising and treatment surrogates, but the simulated effect sizes do not transfer automatically.
The conclusion preserves the failed internal branch and requests hospital, neighboring-state, and travel data, but it still calls the external model extremely robust.
Contents, References, table cells, map labels, nomenclature, appendix factor lists, captions, headers, and form furniture must not inflate positive human-language counts.
